# Part 2: Web Scraping

## Question 1: Scrape a Table

### 1. Read the page into R and extract the table as a data frame.

### 2. Clean the column names, remove the row of citywide totals so that 77 rows remain, and convert total population to a numeric value.

### 3. Print the row for West Town, then print five community areas with the largest population.

```{r}
# read the elements into R
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_in_Chicago"
html <- read_html(url) 
# extracting tables from Wikipedia
tables <- html |>
  html_elements("table") |>
  html_table()
# check how many tables were extracted 
length(tables)
#look for population table
tables[[2]]
# select community areas table
community_areas <- tables[[2]]
# clean columns
community_areas <- community_areas |>
  clean_names()
# check names
names(community_areas)
# remove citywide totals row
community_areas <- community_areas |>
  filter(name != "Chicago")
# convert population to numeric (must remove commas)
community_areas <- community_areas |>
  mutate(total_population = as.numeric(str_remove_all(total_population, ",")))
# check if conversion was successful
class(community_areas$total_population)
# print row for West Town & print five community areas with largest pop
community_areas |> 
  filter(name == "West Town")
community_areas |>
  arrange(desc(total_population)) |>
  head(5)
# check total of remaining community areas & display first 6
nrow(community_areas)
head(community_areas)
```

## Question 2: Scrape with CSS Selectors

### 1. Extract three variables using CSS selectors and combine them in a tibble with 20 rows

### 2. Convert price to a numeric variable, then save the table to your repo as books.csv

### Bonus: Add star rating of each book as a number 1 to 5

```{r}
# load books to scrape website
books_url <- "https://books.toscrape.com/"
books_html <- read_html(books_url)

# extract the book titles
book_titles <- books_html |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |>
  html_attr("title")
# check books total
length(book_titles)

# extract book prices
book_prices <- books_html |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod .price_color") |>
  html_text2()
# check price totals
length(book_prices)

# extract book availability
book_availability <- books_html |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod .availability") |>
  html_text2()
# check availability totals
length(book_availability)

# combine into tibble with 20 rows
book_info <- tibble(
  title = book_titles,
  price = book_prices,
  availability = book_availability
)
# show tibble
book_info

# convert price to numeric
book_info <- book_info |>
  mutate(price = as.numeric(str_remove_all(price, "£")))
# confirm price converstion and book totals
class(book_info$price)
nrow(book_info)
head(book_info)

# save to repository as CSV
write_csv(book_info, "books.csv")

# BONUS!!!!
# add book ratings variable
book_ratings <- books_html |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod .star-rating") |>
  html_attr("class")
# remove prefix
book_ratings <- str_remove_all(book_ratings, "star-rating ")
# convert to numeric
book_ratings <- case_when(
  book_ratings == "One" ~ 1,
  book_ratings == "Two" ~ 2,
  book_ratings == "Three" ~ 3,
  book_ratings == "Four" ~ 4,
  book_ratings == "Five" ~ 5)
# add to table
book_info <- book_info |>
  mutate(star_rating = book_ratings)
book_info
# save updated 
write_csv(book_info, "books.csv")
```

# Part 3: Open Data API

### 1. Request the 1,000 most recent service requests in West Town that were created on or after January 1, 2026. 

### 2. Convert the JSON response to a data frame. Print the number of rows and the column names.

### 3. Summarize. [4 points] Count the requests by sr_type and show the 10 most common request types

### 4. In 2 to 3 sentences, say what this summary suggests about service needs in West Town and name one thing the data cannot tell you.

The most frequent 311 requests made in West Town suggests that service needs of that area largely revolve around graffiti removal, rodent management, and parking code enforcement amongst other things. This data does not tell us the severity/significance of the effect the issue being requested has on residents.

### Bonus: For requests with status "Completed", compute the median number of days between
created_date and closed_date for each of the 5 most common request types.

```{r}
# 311 service requests API
url_311 <- ("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json")

# requesting the data
response_311 <- GET(
  url_311,
  query = list(
    community_area = "24",
    `$where` = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
    `$order` = "created_date DESC",
    `$limit` = 1000
  )
)
```

```{r}
# convert json response to dataframe
requests_311 <- fromJSON(content(response_311, "text"))
# check number of rows to ensure 1000
nrow(requests_311)
names(requests_311)

# count requests by service type and display 10 most common
request_counts <- requests_311 |>
  count(sr_type)

#display 10 most common request types
request_counts |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(10)

```

```{r}
# BONUS
# find 5 most common request types
top_5_types <- requests_311 |>
  count(sr_type) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5)
top_5_types

# filter completed, calculate days, and calculate median 
requests_311 |>
  filter(status == "Completed",
         sr_type %in% top_5_types$sr_type) |>
  mutate(days = as.numeric(difftime(closed_date, created_date, units = "days"))) |>
  group_by(sr_type) |>
  summarise(median_days = median(days, na.rm = TRUE))
```

# Part 4: Census API

## Step 1: Identify the variables

Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income, "50% or more": B25070_010E

Median Household Income: B19013_001E

## Step 2: Retrieve the data

## Step 3: Clean and transform

```{r}
# Retreiving 2024 ACS data for Ohio
ohio_acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    rent_burden = "B25070_010",
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    rent_total = "B25070_001"
    ),
  state = "OH",
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5"
)

head(ohio_acs) # check results

# Clean and transform the data
clean_ohioacs <- ohio_acs |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider( # make variable column into seperate columns
    names_from = variable, # create columns from variable categories
    values_from = estimate 
  )

# Calculate severe rent burden rate and sort counties
clean_ohioacs <- clean_ohioacs|>
  mutate(severe_burden_rate = (rent_burden / rent_total) * 100) |> arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))

```

## Bonus: Split the NAME column into separate county and state columns

```{r}
# split name column into county and state columns
ohio_bonus <- clean_ohioacs |> # created seperate df because the new columns replaced the "name" column and I was unable to run the code again fully
  separate(NAME, into = c("county", "state"), sep = ",")

# check that county and state columns were made successfully
head(ohio_bonus)

```

## Step 4: Analyze

1.  Compute the mean and the median severe_burden_rate across counties
2.  Identify the 5 counties with the highest rates and the 5 with the lowest rates

```{r}
# compute mean and median severe rent burden rates
clean_ohioacs |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate = mean(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_mean = median(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# 5 counties with highest rates
head(clean_ohioacs, 5)
# 5 counties with lowest reates
tail(clean_ohioacs, 5)
```

## Step 5: Visualize

1.  Scatterplot of median household income against severe_burden_rate with a regression line, labeled axes, and an informative title.
2.  Bar chart of the top 5 and bottom 5 counties from Step 4, with bars in order

```{r}

# Relationship between MHI and SRB
ggplot(clean_ohioacs, aes(x = median_income, y = severe_burden_rate)) + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + # add regression line
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income and Severe Rent Burden for Ohio",
    x = "Median Household Income ($)",
    y = "Severe Rent Burden Rate (%)"
  )

# Bar chart of top 5 and bottom 5 counties
top5_bottom5_ohio <- bind_rows( # combine top 5 and bottom 5
  head(clean_ohioacs, 5),
  tail(clean_ohioacs, 5)
)
ggplot(top5_bottom5_ohio,
       aes(x = reorder(NAME, severe_burden_rate),
           y = severe_burden_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  coord_flip() + # make bars horizontal so labels can be read
  theme_light() +
  labs(
    title = "Top and Bottom 5 Severe Rent Burden by Ohio Counties",
    x = "County",
    y = "Severe Rent Burden Rate Percentage"
  )
```
